One-sentence judgment: cartographers and photogrammetrists are not about 'drawing a good-looking map' — they turn source data such as survey records, aerial photographs, satellite imagery, and base maps into spatial data and map products whose scale, projection, coordinates, and feature representation can all be explained, reviewed, and updated: gathering and checking source data, deciding which source material is usable, identifying and scaling and orienting geodetic points and elevations and terrain features using standard mathematical formulas, extracting surface features with stereo plotting and photogrammetric and remote sensing methods, determining map content and layout and scale and projection and color production standards, compiling and revising maps and charts and three-dimensional terrain models, building and updating digital databases, and checking the completeness and accuracy of the final product before delivery. O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone Four (considerable preparation, SVP range 7.0 to below 8.0), the interest code is CIR (conventional, investigative, realistic), and this occupation's page is labeled Bright Outlook. The core boundary is: map and boundary representation often involves legal and administrative basis and ownership records, and the management of classified geographic information and survey results and map content review and professional signing each have public rules and institutional requirements; this occupation's output is a review record of source data and mapping standards and does not replace the determinations of legal and administrative and ownership authorities, nor does it replace the professional signing and acceptance of authorized personnel.

Signals to keep exploring: you can patiently check the version and units and coordinate system of source data, you are willing to spend long periods at a computer processing data and graphics (the O*NET work context shows 83% sitting continuously or almost continuously, 98% working indoors every day, 87% using email every day, 87% considering precision or accuracy extremely important, and a work activity importance of 92 on 'using computers'), you can stop and check the original records rather than immediately filling in a plausible-looking value when data are inconsistent or missing, you are willing to write the reason and basis for every determination and change into a traceable record, and you can accept the long-term demand for detail and patience that 'map and boundary representation must withstand questioning' places on you.

Conditions for pausing large investments first: you have not yet completed a full closed-loop exercise from source data checking through coordinate and projection and unit verification, feature extraction and editing, and mapping standard determination to final product inspection; or you are unwilling to check sources and versions and framings, unwilling to leave a documented basis for determinations per the standards, or unwilling to stop and escalate rather than guessing and filling in when data are inconsistent; also, being able to produce a map with some mapping software must not be treated as proof of spatial data quality determination, interpretation of boundary and ownership basis, and mapping standard formulation ability.

Education, qualification, and authorization must be verified separately: O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone Four (considerable preparation, SVP range 7.0 to below 8.0), and the education survey shows 36% of respondents saying a postsecondary certificate is needed, 30% a bachelor's degree, and 11% that some college without a degree is sufficient; this occupation's page lists 12 certifications (including the American Society for Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing Certified Photogrammetrist (ASPRS), Certified Mapping Scientist, GIS/LIS (ASPRS), Certified Photogrammetric Technologist, and Certified Mapping Scientist, Remote Sensing (ASPRS), the Geographic Information Systems Certification Institute Geographic Information Systems Professional, and the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency GEOINT Professional Certification Cartography and GEOINT Professional Certification Imagery Science), and lists 2 occupation titles approved by the U.S. Department of Labor for registered apprenticeship (Drafter, Cartographic and Geospatial Specialist). On the U.S. side, the occupation usually does not require a uniform license, but some states and employers have separate registration or qualification requirements for surveying and boundary-related work; in mainland China, surveying and mapping activities and map compilation and the management of classified survey results are governed by public rules such as the Surveying and Mapping Law of the People's Republic of China and the Map Management Regulations, and surveying qualifications are obtained by units that meet the corresponding conditions. Education and training, industry certification, statutory qualifications and work qualifications, position hiring and authorization, and professional signing and acceptance and deliverable responsibility are five different things.

One sentence: this is a position that turns 'whether the data source, coordinates and projection, feature representation, and boundary basis of this spatial dataset and map can be explained clearly' into reviewable evidence, with outputs being source data and version check records, coordinate and projection and unit verification records, feature extraction and editing records, mapping standard and layout notes, data quality and completeness check records, and database and metadata version records; it is not a legal or administrative or ownership determination role, nor does it replace the professional signing and determination by authorized personnel of boundaries and ownership and map content and classified results. The U.S. wages and employment are a public statistical framing, while for mainland China this route obtained no occupation-level statistical framing, and this page shows the gap rather than filling in proxy values.

The work of this occupation falls into three categories: first, data acquisition and processing (gathering aerial photographs and survey records and reports and base maps, consulting legal records to determine property boundaries, applying standard mathematical formulas to identify and scale and orient geodetic points and elevations and terrain features, collecting surface feature data with aerial photography and remote sensing techniques, and analyzing and interpreting ground survey and image data); second, cartographic design and map production (determining map content and layout as well as scale and size and projection and color and other production standards, compiling and revising delineated drawings and charts and detail drawings and three-dimensional terrain models, supervising production per the standards, and building and updating digital databases); third, inspection and updating (checking the completeness and accuracy of the final product, revising existing maps and charts and making necessary corrections, verifying sources and versions and framings, and recording the basis for determinations and handing over). All three share the same chain centered on 'traceable sources, correct coordinates and projection and units, and reviewable mapping standards'.
Data acquisition and processing

Gather and check source data and versions → consult legal and administrative records to determine the boundary basis → verify the coordinate system and projection and units and elevation datum → apply standard mathematical formulas to identify and scale and orient control points and terrain features → extract surface features with aerial photography and remote sensing methods and organize them into usable data → produce source and verification records
Cartographic design and map production

Determine map content and purpose and scale and projection and color standards → design the layout and legend and annotation rules → edit and compile delineated drawings and charts and detail drawings and three-dimensional terrain models → build and update digital databases and metadata → supervise production per the standards and keep feature representation consistent → output the map and data deliverables and retain version records

Check the completeness and accuracy of the final product and compare it item by item against the sources → verify whether feature positions and attributes and annotations match the sources → re-verify coordinates and projection and units and accuracy statements → record the problems found and the reasons for changes and the version → escalate questions beyond authority or involving boundaries and ownership and classified content to authorized personnel → complete handover and archiving

Cartographers and photogrammetrists center on the compilation and quality and representation of spatial data and map products; information systems technical specialists and technicians specialize in the operation and maintenance of geographic information systems and data entry and updating and map output operations, surveyors specialize in field surveying and field records and point results, surveying and mapping technicians specialize in technical assistance such as graphic editing and data organizing under direction, remote sensing scientists and remote sensing technologists specialize in the processing and information extraction and monitoring analysis of satellite and aerial imagery, data scientists specialize in statistical and machine learning modeling and prediction, and database architects specialize in general database structure and governance and performance. Similar names or sharing a spatial information chain do not mean that data source determination, mapping standards, and professional signing and acceptance responsibility are interchangeable.
Core purpose

To bring spatial data and map products to requirements in traceable sources and correct coordinates and projection and units and consistent feature representation and mapping standards: source and version checks keep data traceable, verification and editing records keep the process reviewable, and completeness checks and handover keep problems from being carried past delivery and use.
Main subjects and basis

The subjects are aerial photographs and satellite imagery, ground survey records and point results, base maps and charts, boundary information contained in legal and administrative and ownership records, control point and elevation and terrain and surface feature data, and the spatial databases and maps and charts and three-dimensional terrain models and metadata compiled from them; the cooperating parties include the commissioning party and user departments, surveying and remote sensing crews, software and data suppliers, adjacent professional roles, and reviewers and acceptance personnel. The basis is the version and accuracy and coverage statements of the source data, the coordinate system and projection and elevation datum and unit provisions, the mapping standards for map content and purpose and scale, the public records of boundary and ownership basis, and the statutory requirements and institutional procedures for the management of survey results and classified geographic information and map content.
Core process

Gather and check source data, consult legal and administrative records, verify the coordinate system and projection and units, identify and orient control points and terrain features, extract and edit surface features, determine mapping standards and layout, build and update databases and metadata, compile and revise drawings, check completeness and accuracy, and record and hand over and archive.
Main outputs

Source data and version check records, coordinate and projection and unit verification records, feature extraction and editing records, mapping standard and layout and legend notes, spatial database and metadata version records, finished maps and charts and three-dimensional terrain models, data quality and completeness check records, and revision and correction records and handover and archiving records.
Accountable parties

This occupation may carry source selection and coordinate and projection verification and feature representation and map production and quality checking; a supplier's accuracy statement does not exempt the user from verification or the surveying unit from responsibility for deliverable quality. Legal determination of boundaries and signing and acceptance of deliverables follow statutory requirements and the division of position authority; public map review and approval of classified results are handled under Chinese regulations and cannot be uniformly reduced to an internal decision by authorized personnel. When a source or spatial reference is in doubt, pause your related processing and report.
Admission and permits

Independent tasks and data access and deliverable signing and external release must each be verified for legal conditions and unit qualifications and individual qualifications and data licenses and position authority; training records and written institutional authorization cannot by themselves create statutory qualifications or approvals. The BLS OOH notes that licensing requirements may vary by state and employer and duties, and that certification is usually optional; this round did not verify the specific requirements state by state and does not treat 'usually no uniform license' as a conclusion that no license is needed. Articles 27—29 of China's Surveying and Mapping Law require units to obtain the corresponding surveying qualification and work within the licensed scope; Articles 30—31 concern professional technical personnel practice qualification conditions and surveying work certificates respectively, and unit qualifications cannot replace individual conditions. Article 34 requires approval through statutory procedures when classified results are provided externally, and Article 39 requires surveying units to be responsible for deliverable quality. Article 7 of the Map Management Regulations sets the qualification of map compiling units; Article 13 requires lawful use of classified survey results that have undergone confidentiality technical processing by the designated competent department; Articles 15—16 require maps released to the public to be submitted for review to the competent department with review authority as provided, with the exception of maps with simple content such as scenic area maps and street maps and subway line maps. Internal authorization does not replace statutory review; the qualification grade and individual qualifications and confidentiality approval applicable to specific business and the target U.S. state rules must still be verified separately.
Conclusion boundaries

The compilation and verification records are used to trace source versions, spatial references, accuracy statements, reasons for adoption, and the revision process; the records do not equal a legal boundary determination or deliverable acceptance. The statutory review of public maps in China and the conditions for using classified results are verified separately, and internal institutional review does not replace competent department review.

Before starting, verify at least six items: job duties (leaning toward data acquisition and processing, cartographic design and map production, three-dimensional and photogrammetric work, remote sensing and image analysis, or data governance and metadata), the data categories you may handle independently and whether classified or restricted geographic information is involved and the corresponding approval and authorization, whether field verification and site reconnaissance must be carried, who provides the software and data platforms and licenses, the signing and release authority and review process for deliverables, and the allocation of data source and accuracy responsibility and rework and correction responsibility.
Occupational framing

O*NET-SOC 17-1021.00 (SOC 17-1021, cartographers and photogrammetrists within the architecture and engineering major group), listed as Job Zone Four (considerable preparation, SVP range 7.0 to below 8.0), and this occupation's page is labeled Bright Outlook; the interest code is CIR (conventional 72, investigative 70, realistic 60), and the specific interest fields corresponding to conventional and investigative are led by mathematics and statistics (63) and information technology (59) and engineering (31) and physical science (27); the O*NET industry distribution shows 48% of this occupation in government, 34% in professional scientific and technical services, and 18% in other industries. The official U.S. scope of 17-1021.00 is researching, compiling, and producing maps and other spatial data in digital or graphic form, and possibly using geographic information systems and designing and evaluating the algorithms and data structures and user interfaces of GIS and cartographic systems. This round did not establish a one-to-one correspondence between a Chinese subcategory and O*NET-SOC17-1021.00, and the related duties may fall within surveying and geographic information services and territorial spatial planning and cartography and geographic information positions and must be judged by the position's actual duties and qualifications and institutional authorization; the Chinese page language does not constitute an equivalent Chinese occupation or wage mapping.
Education and training pathways

The typical BLS entry classification for SOC17-1021 is a bachelor's degree, no related work experience, and no typical on-the-job training; the OOH notes that workers usually study cartography, geography, geomatics, surveying, or a related field. The O*NET Job Zone4 statement of mostly four-year degrees and several years of experience or training is a general level description and cannot replace this occupation's classification; the education figures 36%/30%/11% are respondents' judgments about the education new hires need (postsecondary certificate / bachelor's / some college no degree), not the educational composition of practitioners. The certification directory has 12 items, and the detail page separately lists the two registered apprenticeship occupation titles Drafter, Cartographic and Geospatial Specialist; the specific open programs and enrollment and costs and maintenance conditions were not verified. No uniform evidence on Chinese target position education and course requirements was obtained, so they are verified against the actual duties.
Methods and tools

The O*NET detail page has 26 categories of software skills; the separate Hot Technologies page has 24 specific hiring technologies, and ArcGIS appears in Lightcast2025 U.S. job postings at a frequency of 62%, while no frequency is provided for the rest. The number of categories, the number of technology items, and the frequency are not the same indicator and cannot be treated as a list that every individual must master or that institutions have deployed. Methods include interpretation of aerial and satellite imagery, stereo plotting, coordinate projection and elevation datum verification, and GIS/CAD and spatial database processing; some positions collect or verify field data.
Safety and work permits

The work is mainly indoor data processing but may include field verification. The O*NET work context shows: 98% working indoors in a controlled environment every day; 83% sitting continuously or almost continuously; 87% using email every day; 87% considering precision or accuracy extremely important; 71% having face-to-face discussions every day; 68% having telephone conversations every day; 56% in continuous contact with others; 50% continuously using hands to handle and control objects and tools; 37% facing time pressure every day; 53% performing repetitive motions continuously; 46% considering coordinating or leading others extremely important; 29% having a lot of freedom in how to make decisions and 51% some freedom; 42% considering the work highly automated; 24% exposed to distracting or uncomfortable noise every day; 11% considering the consequences of error extremely serious and 16% very serious. Field verification must follow institutional procedures and working condition requirements, and on-site work and equipment use and data carrying and classified information management requirements must be complied with.
Training and regulatory requirements

The BLS OOH notes that licensing requirements may vary by state and employer and duties, and that certification is usually optional; this round did not verify the specific requirements state by state and does not treat 'usually no uniform license' as a conclusion that no license is needed. Articles 27—29 of China's Surveying and Mapping Law require units to obtain the corresponding surveying qualification and work within the licensed scope; Articles 30—31 concern professional technical personnel practice qualification conditions and surveying work certificates respectively, and unit qualifications cannot replace individual conditions. Article 34 requires approval through statutory procedures when classified results are provided externally, and Article 39 requires surveying units to be responsible for deliverable quality. Article 7 of the Map Management Regulations sets the qualification of map compiling units; Article 13 requires lawful use of classified survey results that have undergone confidentiality technical processing by the designated competent department; Articles 15—16 require maps released to the public to be submitted for review to the competent department with review authority as provided, with the exception of maps with simple content such as scenic area maps and street maps and subway line maps. Internal authorization does not replace statutory review; the qualification grade and individual qualifications and confidentiality approval applicable to specific business and the target U.S. state rules must still be verified separately.
Pay and hours

The BLS OOH notes that most work is full-time and that some positions require field work with possibly longer field days; O*NET shows NET37% facing time pressure every day, 83% sitting continuously, and 98% working indoors in a controlled environment every day. The 2025 U.S. national annual wages P10/P25/P50/P75/P90 are 53,740/65,670/81,390/101,960/126,950 USD; the corresponding hourly wages are 25.84/31.57/39.13/49.02/61.03 USD. Percentiles do not represent starting pay or seniority or personal take-home income. BLS SOC17-1021: 2025 employment 14,700, 2035 projection 15,700, an official net change of 1,100 and growth of 7.4%, with about 900 average annual openings over 2025—2035, and 1.2% self-employed in 2025. The headcounts in the table are rounded and the endpoint difference cannot be used to override the official net change; openings include replacement needs from transfers out and labor force exits and do not equal net growth or an AI-driven change. The 2025 NBS average annual wage in scientific research and technical services: 182,064 yuan for urban non-private units and 83,560 yuan for private units (pretax). This is an industry reference matched to the surveying and geographic information professional services direction, mixing all positions in the industry, and is not the average or monthly wage range or personal offer for cartographers and photogrammetrists. Comparing opportunities should also verify data and software costs, field arrangements, signing and release, and rework and correction responsibility.

Cartographers and photogrammetrists (O*NET-SOC 17-1021.00, Cartographers and Photogrammetrists) research, study, and prepare maps and other spatial data in digital or graphic form for legal, social, political, educational, and design purposes; they may work with geographic information systems (GIS) and may design and evaluate the algorithms, data structures, and user interfaces of GIS and mapping systems; they may collect, analyze, and interpret geographic information provided by geodetic surveys, aerial photographs, and satellite data. Daily work includes: using aerial photographs and stereo plotting and computer graphics equipment to extract aerial photograph details such as control points, drainage, and terrain and cultural features, and to compile and revise delineated drawings, charts, tables, detail drawings, and three-dimensional terrain models; gathering the data needed to compile maps, including aerial photographs, survey records, reports, and base maps; consulting legal records to determine local, national, and international boundaries; applying standard mathematical formulas to identify, scale, and orient geodetic points, elevations, and other plane or terrain features; using aerial photography and other digital remote sensing techniques to collect information about specific features of the earth; analyzing and studying ground survey and report and aerial photograph and satellite imagery data to compile topographic maps, aerial photograph mosaics, and related charts; determining map content and layout as well as scale, size, projection, and color and other production standards, and supervising production to comply with the standards; deciding which source material is usable; selecting the aerial photography and remote sensing methods and drafting equipment needed to meet accuracy and precision requirements; building and updating digital databases; revising existing maps and charts and making necessary corrections and adjustments; and checking the completeness and accuracy of the final product. It carries responsibility for source determination and correct coordinates and projection and units and feature representation and mapping standards and records, but does not replace legal and administrative and ownership determinations, nor does it replace the professional signing and acceptance of authorized personnel.

The median means half of workers earn above and half below that value; it is not an entry-level wage or a starting-salary promise; the occupation usually requires a four-year bachelor's degree or equivalent preparation, and wage percentiles do not represent an individual's job offer.

Mainland China side: this round obtained no exact nationwide median or percentiles or uniform starting wage for this occupation; this page separately gives the background of the 2025 pretax industry average wages in scientific research and technical services of 182,064 yuan/year for non-private units and 83,560 yuan/year for private units. The industry covers all positions and is not this occupation's wage or an individual income floor or ceiling or a recruitment offer, and is not converted from U.S. figures. This round did not establish a reliable one-to-one correspondence with O*NET17-1021.00 for a Chinese occupational subcategory, and it cannot be asserted from this that related occupations do not exist.

Industry distribution and employment background: the O*NET industry distribution shows 48% of this occupation in government, 34% in professional scientific and technical services, and 18% in other industries; the BLS framing displayed by O*NET is about 14,700 in 2025, with 2025—2035 projected growth of 7.4% (7% in the OOH, Much faster than average) and about 900 average annual job openings (including replacement needs such as turnover and retirement); position demand is affected by public projects related to geographic information and surveying and territorial space and planning, updates in data collection technology such as remote sensing and drones, expanded applications such as digital twins and location services, and the supply of people with spatial data quality and mapping standards and data processing ability. This occupation's page is labeled Bright Outlook; an outlook label is a direction hint at the occupational group level and not a personal success guarantee.

Tool signals and abilities: the detail page has 26 categories of software skills, and Hot Technologies separately lists 24 specific hiring technologies (shown at the Hot Technologies entry, where ESRI ArcGIS software appears at a share of 62% while no frequency is marked for the rest; Lightcast 2025 U.S. job postings); work activities center on getting information (97), using computers (92), evaluating information to determine compliance with standards (81), decision making and problem solving (81), identifying objects and actions and events (80), updating and using relevant knowledge (80), and documenting and recording information (79); basic skills center on reading comprehension (75) and critical thinking (63) and writing (63) and active listening (60), with mathematics 47 and science 22; transferable skills center on complex problem solving (53) and judgment and decision making (53) and coordination (50) and social perceptiveness (50) and time management (50); knowledge centers on geography (88) and computers and electronics (81) and English language (64) and design (59) and mathematics (58); the interest code is CIR (conventional, investigative, realistic); work styles center on attention to detail (100) and dependability (73) and inquisitiveness (71) and caution (68).

paragraphs: This page compares cartographers and photogrammetrists with six adjacent directions on the same set of dimensions: occupational direction, core work and outputs, key differences, and which direction each preference is a better fit for. Adjacent directions are described by their own official occupational descriptions and do not mean job titles or work scope and professional signing and acceptance responsibility are interchangeable.

Evidence note: occupational direction and core outputs are based on O*NET-SOC 17-1021.00 and the official descriptions of adjacent entries (U.S. framing); the adjacent occupations listed by this evidence route are database architects, data warehousing specialists, information systems technical specialists and technicians, data scientists, and surveyors, with surveying and mapping technicians and remote sensing scientists and remote sensing technologists as same-chain directions among O*NET related occupations; work scope and professional signing and acceptance responsibility, map content review, and classified geographic information management must be verified separately by each jurisdiction and institution and contract; this page does not present any direction as a shortcut for switching careers.

The table below compares the differences in duties and outputs between cartographers and photogrammetrists and adjacent directions; the basis for judgment is the main outputs, what the work is accountable for, and the required qualifications and authorization, not how similar the job titles sound.

This direction specializes in the operation and maintenance of existing systems and data entry and updating, and the work scope and map output standards are given by the established system; this occupation additionally carries source determination, coordinate and projection and accuracy design, and responsibility for explaining the boundary and ownership basis.

If you would rather do data maintenance and map output and system operation under established standards, examine information systems technical specialists and technicians first; if you would rather be responsible for source determination and cartographic design and the boundary basis, examine this occupation first.

Operating and maintaining geographic information systems, entering and updating spatial data layers, and producing maps and doing data checks per the established standards, with outputs being usable geographic information datasets and map products.
Information systems technical specialists and technicians

Surveyors use field measurement and field records as first-hand evidence and are responsible for field accuracy; this occupation mostly uses existing survey and image and satellite data for mapping and spatial analysis, with field work usually limited to verification and supplementation.

If you would rather run field work and operate surveying instruments and be responsible for field results, examine surveyors first; if you would rather do data processing and cartographic design and spatial analysis, examine this occupation first.
Determining boundaries and terrain and engineering points through field measurement and records, with outputs being survey records and point results and boundary evidence.
Surveyors

This direction is mainly technical assistance, and the work scope and signing authority are limited by position authorization; this occupation carries responsibility for the complete chain from data source determination to mapping standards and inspection.

If you would rather do technical assistance and graphic editing and data organizing, examine surveying and mapping technicians first; if you would rather carry the complete responsibility from data to mapping and inspection, examine this occupation first.
Completing data entry and graphic editing and drawing organizing under the direction of a surveyor or cartographer, with outputs being organized graphic and data deliverables.
Surveying and mapping technicians

This direction specializes in the acquisition and processing and analysis of remote sensing imagery and leans toward science and monitoring; this occupation centers on the compilation and mapping of maps and spatial data and the representation of boundaries and ownership.

If you would rather do image processing and remote sensing monitoring analysis, examine remote sensing scientists and remote sensing technologists first; if you would rather do map compilation and spatial data products and mapping standards, examine this occupation first.

Using satellite and aerial remote sensing data for image processing and information extraction and environmental and surface monitoring analysis, with outputs being imagery products and analytical conclusions.

paragraphs: Boundary: this section describes occupational risk and work responsibility boundaries, not an evaluation of individuals or institutions; specific procedures and handling processes are determined by the applicable jurisdiction, data sources and accuracy statements, institutional data and confidentiality management systems and the commissioning contract.

Direct answer: the main risks include conclusions being distorted because source data versions and coverage are inconsistent or unreliable; positions and attributes being misplaced because of errors in coordinate systems, projections, units, elevation datums and scale conversion; finished products being unusable because features, attributes and annotations do not match the source; leakage and out-of-scope use of classified or restricted geographic information and client data; a responsibility vacuum caused by handing source judgment, accuracy statements and product signing to tools or unauthorized people; and making out-of-scope determinations about boundaries and ownership. Controls depend on checking sources and versions with documented evidence, dual verification of coordinate systems, projections, units and dimensions, consistency checks between mapping standards and map presentation, managing classified and restricted data according to institutional rules, and a clear version, correction and escalation path.

Check tasks and work context against O*NET; exposure percentages are not accident rates. For Chinese unit qualifications, individual conditions, classified products and public map requirements, check Articles 27—39 of the Surveying and Mapping Law and Articles 7—16 of the Regulation on Map Management. The controls are editorial suggestions tied to the tasks, and the specific process must be checked against the jurisdiction and project rules.
Cartographers and photogrammetrists themselves: the data source checking role

Source data versions and coverage being inconsistent or unreliable distorts conclusions and affects downstream decisions (87% consider precision or accuracy extremely important; 11% consider the consequences of error extremely serious and 16% very serious).

Register the source, version, accuracy and coverage of each item and keep the original provenance; for inconsistencies, re-check the original records before deciding whether to adopt them; leave unverifiable sources blank and mark them as insufficient evidence rather than filling them with guesses.
Adopting a single dataset at hand with no version or source marked in order to meet a deadline, or overlaying two datasets with different coverage without explaining the differences.
Cartographers and photogrammetrists themselves: the data verification role

Errors in coordinate systems, projections, units, elevation datums and scale conversion cause features to be misplaced, attributes to mismatch and products to be unusable (87% consider precision or accuracy extremely important).

Before mapping, determine the coordinate system, projection, elevation datum and units and put them in writing; double-check conversions and position results and keep verification records; when inconsistencies are found, stop first and re-check the source and parameters rather than carrying erroneous results into mapping and release.
Mixing data in different coordinate systems or elevation datums without declaring it, or filling in units by convention without checking the source documentation.
Cartographers and photogrammetrists themselves: the information security management role
Mishandling classified or restricted geographic information, client-commissioned data and internal maps leads to confidentiality and compliance consequences.

First check the data source, classification, licence, storage and external transmission permissions; use classified surveying and mapping products according to statutory procedure, obtain approval as required before providing them externally, and check the confidentiality technical processing conditions of the designated department for mapping. Internal authorization does not replace statutory approval; do not input restricted data into unapproved external tools, and if anomalies are found, pause the relevant processing you are doing and report it.
Uploading restricted data to unapproved online tools for convenience, or sending maps containing sensitive locations to public groups and social platforms.
Cartographers and photogrammetrists themselves: the product review and delivery role

Features, attributes and annotations not matching the source, or an incomplete finished product, carry problems past delivery and into use (87% consider precision or accuracy extremely important; 29% have a lot of freedom in how they make decisions).

Before delivery, check completeness and accuracy item by item against a checklist and against the source; write the problems found, the reasons for changes and the version into a record; escalate matters that cannot be confirmed to authorized personnel rather than deciding them yourself.
Skipping finished-product checks to meet a deadline, or leaving inconsistencies found to the user to just use for now.
Cartographers and photogrammetrists themselves: the professional signing role
Giving source determination and accuracy statements and deliverable signing to tools or unauthorized people creates a responsibility vacuum and untraceability.

Source selection and quality verification can be part of this occupation's tasks and are documented per job responsibilities; the organization is responsible for the quality of its surveying and mapping products. For public maps, first check whether review by the statutory competent department is required and who must submit it; internal signing or acceptance does not replace it; when release is uncertain, pause the relevant steps you are doing and report it.
Publishing maps or data products in the name of the organization without authorization, or verbally promising accuracy and coverage.
Cartographers and photogrammetrists themselves: boundary and ownership related work

Making determinations about boundaries and ownership beyond your duties creates liability that is hard to bear in a dispute (public records involving legal, administrative and ownership evidence are involved).

Only organize and present the evidence based on public records and note the source and version; refer matters involving determinations to the competent legal, administrative and ownership authorities or authorized bodies; put conditions and exceptions in writing; when uncertain, report to authorized personnel before answering.

BLS classifies the typical entry-level preparation for SOC17-1021 as a bachelor's degree, no related work experience and no typical on-the-job training; OOH notes that people usually study cartography, geography, geomatics, surveying or a related field. The majority of four-year degrees plus several years of experience or training shown for O*NET Job Zone4 is a zone-level general description and cannot replace the classification for this occupation; the education figures of 36%/30%/11% are respondents' judgments about the education new hires need (postsecondary certificate/bachelor's degree/some college, no degree) and are not the educational attainment of incumbents. The certification directory lists 12 items, and the detail page additionally lists two registered apprenticeship occupation titles, Drafter, Cartographic and Geospatial Specialist; the specific open programs, enrollment, costs and maintenance conditions were not verified. BLS OOH notes that licensing requirements may vary by state, employer and duties, and that certification is usually optional; this round did not check the specific requirements state by state, and usually no unified licence is not treated as a no-licence conclusion. China's Surveying and Mapping Law, Articles 27—29, requires units to obtain the corresponding surveying and mapping qualification and to work within the licensed scope; Articles 30—31 concern the practice qualification conditions of professional and technical personnel and surveying and mapping work certificates respectively, and unit qualification cannot replace individual conditions. Article 34 requires that classified products be provided externally according to statutory procedure for approval, and Article 39 requires surveying and mapping units to be responsible for product quality. Article 7 of the Regulation on Map Management sets out the qualification of map compilation units; Article 13 requires lawful use of classified surveying and mapping products that have undergone confidentiality technical processing by the designated competent department; Articles 15—16 require maps released to the public to be submitted for review to the competent department with review authority as required, except for simple maps such as scenic area maps, street block maps and subway line maps. Internal authorization does not replace statutory review; the qualification level applicable to specific business, individual qualifications, confidentiality approval and the target U.S. state rules still need to be checked separately.

Qualification boundaries: education and training, industry certification and apprenticeship experience, statutory qualification and practice eligibility (related to surveying and mapping and classified products), job hiring and authorization, and professional signing, acceptance and product delivery responsibility are different states, and none can be automatically inferred from another.

The BLS OOH notes that licensing requirements may vary by state and employer and duties, and that certification is usually optional; this round did not verify the specific requirements state by state and does not treat 'usually no uniform license' as a conclusion that no license is needed. Articles 27—29 of China's Surveying and Mapping Law require units to obtain the corresponding surveying qualification and work within the licensed scope; Articles 30—31 concern professional technical personnel practice qualification conditions and surveying work certificates respectively, and unit qualifications cannot replace individual conditions. Article 34 requires approval through statutory procedures when classified results are provided externally, and Article 39 requires surveying units to be responsible for deliverable quality. Article 7 of the Map Management Regulations sets the qualification of map compiling units; Article 13 requires lawful use of classified survey results that have undergone confidentiality technical processing by the designated competent department; Articles 15—16 require maps released to the public to be submitted for review to the competent department with review authority as provided, with the exception of maps with simple content such as scenic area maps and street maps and subway line maps. entries.answer: Research, compile and produce maps and other spatial data in digital or graphic form: gather the aerial photographs, survey records, reports and source maps needed to compile a map, and consult legal records to determine boundaries; apply standard mathematical formulas to identify, scale and orient geodetic points, elevations and other planimetric or topographic features; use aerial photography and other digital remote sensing techniques to collect information about specific features of the earth; analyze and study ground survey, report, aerial photograph and satellite imagery data to compile topographic maps, aerial photograph mosaics and related charts; use stereoplotting and computer graphics equipment to extract control points, hydrography, terrain and cultural features and to compile and revise tracings, charts, detailed maps and three-dimensional terrain models; determine map content and layout and production standards such as scale, size, projection and color, and supervise production; decide which source materials can be adopted; choose aerial photography and remote sensing methods and drafting equipment that meet precision and accuracy requirements; build and update digital databases; revise existing maps and charts and make necessary corrections; and check the completeness and accuracy of the final product.
entries.question: What do cartographers and photogrammetrists do every day?

entries.answer: The main risks include conclusions being distorted because source data versions and coverage are inconsistent or unreliable; positions and attributes being misplaced because of errors in coordinate systems, projections, units, elevation datums and scale conversion; finished products being unusable because features, attributes and annotations do not match the source; leakage and out-of-scope use of classified or restricted geographic information and client data; a responsibility vacuum caused by handing source judgment, accuracy statements and product signing to tools or unauthorized people; and making out-of-scope determinations about boundaries and ownership. Controls depend on checking sources and versions with documented evidence, dual verification of coordinate systems, projections, units and dimensions, consistency checks between mapping standards and map presentation, managing classified and restricted data according to institutional rules, and a clear version, correction and escalation path.
entries.question: What risks should I pay attention to in advance in this job?

entries.answer: The fit signals are being able to check sources, versions, coordinate systems, projections and units clearly, being able to maintain detail accuracy while sitting and facing a screen for long periods, and being willing to document the basis for decisions and changes to standard and to escalate promptly when uncertain; the key is whether you have reviewable source and version check records, coordinate, projection and unit verification records, feature extraction and editing records and quality control records, rather than only being able to produce a map with some mapping software or a piece of project experience.
entries.question: How do I judge whether this job suits me?

entries.answer: Data gathering and organization, drafting source lists and metadata, preliminary feature extraction screening, first drafts of map annotations and field mapping, organizing record and explanatory text, and organizing checklists and version records can all be assisted; source judgment, coordinate systems, projections, units and accuracy statements, feature representation and mapping standard decisions, completeness and accuracy determination, and professional signing and release are still checked and owned by authorized personnel.
entries.question: Which steps will AI and automation change?

entries.answer: The version, accuracy and coverage of source data, the actual conventions for coordinate systems, projections and elevation datums, the consistency of feature positions, attributes and annotations with the source, mapping standards and map presentation, product completeness and accuracy, and the interpretation of boundary and ownership evidence and product signing and release must all be completed and documented by authorized or qualified people.
entries.question: Which steps must keep human checks?

entries.answer: You need to check separately the education and major threshold (O*NET lists it as Job Zone Four; in the education survey 36% think a postsecondary education certificate is needed, 30% think a bachelor's degree is needed and 11% think having attended college without earning a degree is enough), industry certification and apprenticeship experience (the occupation page lists 12 certifications and 2 registered apprenticeship positions), statutory qualification and practice eligibility (related to surveying and mapping and classified products), and job authorization and data usage scope; this occupation usually does not require a unified licence, and surveying and mapping activities, map compilation and classified surveying and mapping product management in Chinese mainland have separate public rules, and neither education nor training automatically grants data usage scope or the right to decide professional signing and product acceptance.

subject.name: Cartographers and Photogrammetrists
subject.summary: This page entry corresponds to cartographers and photogrammetrists (O*NET-SOC 17-1021.00, Cartographers and Photogrammetrists): researching, compiling and producing maps and other spatial data in digital or graphic form, possibly using geographic information systems and designing and evaluating the algorithms, data structures and user interfaces of GIS and mapping systems — gathering and checking source data, consulting legal records to determine boundaries, applying standard mathematical formulas to identify, scale and orient geodetic points, elevations and terrain features, using aerial photography, remote sensing and stereoplotting methods to extract and edit surface features, determining map content and layout and production standards such as scale, projection and color, building and updating digital databases, revising existing maps and checking product completeness and accuracy; the work is mainly indoor data processing (98% work indoors every day, 83% sit continuously or almost continuously, 87% consider precision or accuracy extremely important, 37% face time pressure every day), and its duties do not replace legal, administrative and ownership determinations, nor do they replace professional signing and product acceptance by authorized personnel; the occupation page marks Bright Outlook.
